title: Masked with Matthew Arnold’s face
html_source: Matthew Arnold was an Oxford don who argued for a renewed religious faith and an adoption of classical aesthetics and morals, particularly representative of mainstream Victorian intellectual concerns. A main theme Joyce borrows from his has to do with the effects of Hebraism and Hellenism. He writes: “At the bottom of both the Greek and the Hebrew notion is the desire, native in man, for reason and the will of God, the feeling after the universal order, — in a word, the love of God. But, while Hebraism seizes upon certain plain, capital intimations of the universal order, and rivets itself, one may say, with unequalled grandeur of earnestness and intensity on the study and observance of them, the bent of Hellenism is to follow, with flexible activity, the whole play of the universal order, to be apprehensive of missing any part of it, of sacrificing one part to another, to slip away from resting in this or that intimation of it, however capital.” The term “Hebraism” is used generally to infer the benefits and moral constraints of religion, while “Hellenism” refers to the “perfecting” effects of high culture. This is a significant and involved theme for Joyce, and to determine his intentions for its use is subject to discussion. Clearly drunkenness is not something Arnold would condone.
